q: What is integration in Salesforce and what are the main types?
alt: What do you mean by Salesforce integration?
Explain the different types of integration in Salesforce
how do you connect salesforce with other systems
What are inbound and outbound integrations?
a: Integration just means connecting Salesforce with other systems so data and processes stay in sync. I think of it in two directions. Outbound is when Salesforce calls an external system, using Apex callouts, outbound messages or events. Inbound is when an external system calls Salesforce, through the REST, SOAP, Bulk or Pub/Sub APIs, or a custom Apex REST service. Then by style there are three types. Data integration keeps records in sync, like customers matching between Salesforce and the ERP. Process integration is when a business process spans systems, like order to invoice: the order is closed in Salesforce, and the invoice gets raised in the finance system. And UI or virtualization integration is when we show external data inside Salesforce without copying it, for example showing ERP order history on the Account page with Salesforce Connect.
points: Outbound: Salesforce calls out (Apex callout, outbound message, events)
Inbound: external system calls Salesforce APIs or Apex REST/SOAP
Types: data, process, and UI/virtualization integration

q: What is the difference between REST and SOAP?
alt: REST vs SOAP API, which one would you use?
Explain REST and SOAP web services
rest versus soap difference in salesforce
Why is REST preferred over SOAP nowadays?
a: REST is an architectural style. It uses standard HTTP methods like GET, POST, PATCH and DELETE on resources, and usually sends lightweight JSON, so it's simple and fast and works well for mobile and web apps. SOAP is a protocol with a strict XML envelope and a WSDL contract that defines every operation and data type. It's heavier but strongly typed, and some enterprise and legacy systems, like banks or older ERPs, still require it. In Salesforce, I consume SOAP by generating Apex classes from a WSDL, and I consume REST with HttpRequest. Say I'm connecting to a modern shipping API, that's REST, and I'll just send JSON. But if a bank's payment gateway only gives me a WSDL, I'll generate the classes and use SOAP. For new integrations I default to REST unless the other system only offers SOAP.
points: REST: HTTP verbs, resources, JSON (or XML), lightweight
SOAP: XML envelope, WSDL contract, strongly typed
Salesforce consumes SOAP via WSDL2Apex, REST via HttpRequest
Default to REST for new work

a: I use three classes. HttpRequest holds the endpoint, method, headers, body and timeout. Http has the send method that actually makes the call. HttpResponse gives me the status code and body. For the endpoint I always use a Named Credential with the callout: prefix, so the URL and authentication aren't hard-coded and I don't need a Remote Site Setting. Say I'm fetching an exchange rate. I set the endpoint to callout:FX_API/rates?base=USD, method GET, and a timeout, because that API can be slow. After the call I check getStatusCode. If it's 200, I parse the JSON. If it's anything else, I throw a custom exception or log the error. The main thing is failures are never silent, otherwise you find out weeks later that rates haven't updated.

q: What are Remote Site Settings and when do you need them?
alt: Why do we need remote site settings for a callout?
What happens if you call an endpoint without a remote site setting?
remote site setting vs named credential
Do I need remote site settings if I use named credentials?
a: Remote Site Settings is a whitelist of external URLs that Apex is allowed to call. If I make a callout to a URL that isn't registered there, I get an 'Unauthorized endpoint' error. I only need it when I put a raw URL in setEndpoint. If I use a Named Credential, the named credential itself authorizes the endpoint, so no Remote Site Setting is needed. That's one more reason I prefer named credentials. The URL and the authentication live in one place. For example, in the sandbox the named credential points to the vendor's test URL, and in production to the live URL. The Apex code is identical in both, and nobody has to edit code or add remote sites after a refresh.

q: What is a Named Credential and why should you use it?
alt: Why use named credentials instead of hard-coding the URL and password?
Explain named credentials in Salesforce
what is the callout colon syntax
How do you store API credentials securely in Salesforce?
a: A Named Credential stores the endpoint URL of an external system together with how to authenticate to it. So in Apex I just write callout:My_Named_Credential/path, and Salesforce adds the authentication for me. The benefits: security, because secrets aren't in code or custom settings. Maintainability, because I can change the URL per environment without a deployment. And less code, because Salesforce can handle OAuth token refresh automatically. For example, if we call a payment API with OAuth, I don't write any code to get or refresh the token. When it expires, Salesforce gets a new one. Named credentials also work for External Services and Salesforce Connect, not just Apex. And in the current model, the authentication part lives in a separate External Credential.

Apex uses 'callout:Name/path'

q: What is the difference between a Named Credential and an External Credential in the current model?
alt: Explain the new named credential and external credential setup
What is a principal in an external credential?
Why does my callout fail even though the named credential is configured? permission set?
legacy named credentials vs new named credentials
a: In the current model, introduced in Winter '23, the work is split in two. The Named Credential holds the endpoint URL and callout options. The External Credential holds the authentication protocol, like OAuth 2.0, JWT, Basic, AWS Signature V4 or Custom, plus the principals. A principal is the identity used for the call. A named principal means one shared integration identity. A per-user principal means each user authenticates separately. Users only get access when a permission set or profile is mapped to that principal. That's a very common reason callouts fail right after setup. Everything looks configured, but the running user's permission set isn't mapped, so the callout has no credentials. One external credential can serve several named credentials. Legacy named credentials are deprecated, so I build new ones in this model.
points: Named Credential = URL + callout options
External Credential = auth protocol + principals
Named principal (shared) vs per-user principal
Grant principal access through a permission set
Legacy named credentials are deprecated

q: How do you pass an API key to an external system securely?
alt: How do I send an API key header without hard-coding it?
Where do you store API keys in Salesforce?
custom header in named credential with credential formula
Should I store the API key in a custom setting?
a: I don't keep API keys in code, custom labels or plain custom settings. I create an External Credential with the Custom authentication protocol, and add the key as an encrypted authentication parameter on the principal. Then I define a custom header, say X-API-Key, whose value is a $Credential formula referencing that parameter. The Named Credential points to the base URL and uses that external credential. Now the Apex just calls the named credential, and the header is added at runtime. Apex never sees or logs the key. So the key is encrypted, hidden from developers, and an admin can rotate it without a deployment. For example, if the vendor says the key leaked and issues a new one, the admin pastes it into the principal and we're done in five minutes.
points: External Credential with Custom protocol
Store key as an encrypted principal parameter

q: How do you parse a JSON response in Apex?
alt: How do you convert JSON into an Apex object?
Explain JSON.deserialize with a wrapper class
how to read json response from api in apex
What is a wrapper class for JSON parsing?
a: When I know the structure, I create a wrapper class whose property names match the JSON keys, and call JSON.deserialize with that class type. It's type-safe and easy to read, and nested objects or arrays just become nested classes and lists. For example, if the response is an order with a customer object and a list of items, I'd have an Order class with a Customer property and a List of Item. One thing to know: unknown keys are ignored by JSON.deserialize. JSON.deserializeStrict throws an error if the JSON has fields that aren't in the class. So if the vendor adds a new field tomorrow, deserialize keeps working, deserializeStrict breaks. For the reverse, building a request body, I use JSON.serialize. And tools that generate Apex from sample JSON can speed up creating the wrapper.

q: When would you use JSON.deserializeUntyped, and how do you handle JSON keys that are Apex reserved words?
alt: How do you parse dynamic JSON without a wrapper class?
JSON key is a reserved keyword like currency, how to deserialize?
deserialize untyped map string object example
How do you parse JSON when the structure keeps changing?
a: I use JSON.deserializeUntyped when the structure is dynamic, or very large with only a few fields I need, or has keys I can't use as Apex property names. It returns Object, which I cast to Map<String, Object> for objects and List<Object> for arrays, then cast each value. For example, if a response has 80 fields and I only need status and id, I don't build a wrapper for all 80. For reserved words, like a key called currency or limit, one option is deserializeUntyped. Another is to replace the key in the raw string before deserializing into a wrapper, for example renaming currency to currency_x. For building JSON I use JSON.serialize, and passing true as the second argument suppresses null values.

q: What is OAuth 2.0 and how does it work at a high level?
alt: Explain OAuth in simple words
What is an access token and a refresh token?
how does oauth authentication work with salesforce
Why use OAuth instead of username and password?
a: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework. It lets an application access an API on behalf of a user, or on its own behalf, without sharing the user's password with that application. The client app is registered with the authorization server. In Salesforce that's through an External Client App or Connected App, and it gets a client Id and secret, or a certificate. Through one of the OAuth flows, it gets an access token, a short-lived key sent in the Authorization Bearer header on every API call. A refresh token, when issued, lets the app get a new access token without the user logging in again. Scopes limit what the token can do. A simple example: a mobile app logs a rep in once, gets a token with just the api and refresh_token scopes, and keeps working for weeks using the refresh token, without ever seeing her password.
points: Access without sharing passwords
Access token: short-lived, sent as Bearer header
Refresh token: gets new access tokens
Scopes limit what the app can do

q: Which OAuth flows does Salesforce support and when do you use each?
alt: Explain the OAuth flows: web server, JWT, client credentials, device
Which OAuth flow would you use for server to server integration?
difference between jwt bearer flow and client credentials flow
What OAuth flow should a mobile app use?
a: I pick the flow based on who the user is and where the client runs. Web server, or authorization code with PKCE, is for apps where a real user logs in through a browser and the app can keep a secret on its server. JWT bearer is for server-to-server integration with no user interaction, signed with a certificate, acting as a pre-authorized user. Client credentials is also server-to-server, using client Id and secret with a configured run-as user. Device flow is for devices with limited input, like a TV or a CLI. User-agent was used by browser and mobile apps, but code flow with PKCE is the better choice today. Refresh token flow renews access. So, a nightly ERP sync would be JWT bearer, and a customer-facing web portal would be auth code with PKCE. I avoid username-password flow, because it's being phased out.
points: Web server (auth code + PKCE): interactive users
JWT bearer: server-to-server with certificate
Client credentials: server-to-server with run-as user
Device: limited-input devices; refresh token: renew access
Avoid username-password flow

q: How does the OAuth 2.0 JWT bearer flow work with Salesforce?
alt: Explain JWT bearer token flow step by step
How do you set up server to server integration using a certificate?
what goes in the JWT claims for salesforce
JWT flow without user login how does it work
a: The JWT bearer flow is for server-to-server integration where nobody can log in interactively. First I generate a certificate and private key, upload the certificate to the External Client App, enable JWT, and pre-authorize the integration user through admin-approved users with a permission set or profile. The external system builds a JWT. iss is the consumer key, sub is the Salesforce username, aud is the login URL, like login.salesforce.com or test.salesforce.com, and exp is short. It signs that with its private key and posts it to the token endpoint. Salesforce checks the signature with the certificate and returns an access token. No refresh token is issued, the client just creates a new JWT when needed. A common mistake: pointing a sandbox integration at login.salesforce.com in aud, when it should be test.salesforce.com.
points: Certificate uploaded to the app; private key stays with client
Claims: iss = consumer key, sub = username, aud = login URL, exp
User must be pre-authorized (admin-approved)
No refresh token; sign a new JWT each time

q: What is the OAuth client credentials flow and what is the run-as user?
alt: When would you use client credentials flow in Salesforce?
client credentials vs jwt bearer which is better
What user does the client credentials flow run as?
How do you integrate without a user context?
a: The client credentials flow lets a backend system get an access token using only the consumer key and secret, with no user login. But every Salesforce API call needs a user context. So I configure a run-as user on the External Client App, and all calls run with that user's permissions. I make it a dedicated integration user with least privilege, ideally on the Salesforce Integration license, with only the permission sets it needs. For example, if a warehouse system only updates stock levels, the run-as user only gets edit on the product inventory fields, nothing else. Compared with JWT bearer, it's simpler because there's no certificate. But the secret must be stored and rotated carefully. JWT is stronger when the client can manage a private key.
points: Consumer key + secret only, no user interaction
Run-as user defines permissions
Use a dedicated least-privilege integration user
Simpler than JWT, but secret must be protected

q: What is the difference between Connected Apps and External Client Apps?
alt: Should I create a connected app or an external client app?
Why can't I create a new connected app in my org?
What changed with connected apps in Spring 26?
external client app vs connected app
a: Both register an external application to Salesforce for OAuth access, but External Client Apps are now the recommended option. As of Spring '26, creating new connected apps is restricted by default, and you have to contact Salesforce Support if you really need one. Existing connected apps keep working. External Client Apps split developer settings, like OAuth flows, scopes and callback URL, from admin policies, like permitted users, IP relaxation and session policies. They're closed by default, so nothing exists in an org until it's installed. They can be local or packaged with second-generation packaging. They don't support the username-password flow, which is another push toward secure flows. So if a team today asks me to set up a new integration that logs in with username and password, I'd tell them to use an ECA with JWT or client credentials instead. Also note the SOAP API login() is being retired too.
points: New connected app creation restricted since Spring '26
ECA: settings (developer) vs policies (admin) separated
Closed by default; local or 2GP packaged
No username-password flow on ECAs
Existing connected apps still work; SOAP API login() is also being retired

q: How do you expose an Apex class as a REST web service?
alt: Write an Apex REST service with HttpGet

What is the endpoint URL for an Apex REST class?
a: I annotate a global class with @RestResource and a urlMapping, and add global static methods annotated with @HttpGet, @HttpPost, @HttpPut, @HttpPatch or @HttpDelete. The external system calls /services/apexrest/ followed by my mapping, with an OAuth access token. For example, with urlMapping '/orders/*', a GET to /services/apexrest/orders/12345 hits my @HttpGet method. I use with sharing and user-mode queries so the integration user's permissions are respected. And I only build custom Apex REST when the standard REST API can't do the job. A typical reason is multi-object logic in one call, like creating an account, contact and opportunity together and applying business rules.

a: For full control I make the @HttpPost method return void. I read RestContext.request.requestBody as a Blob, convert it to a string, and deserialize it into a wrapper class. Say the caller posts a new order but leaves out the customer number. Instead of a raw Salesforce exception, they get a 400 with a body like code MISSING_FIELD and a clear message. Returning a consistent error structure makes life much easier for the calling team, because they can handle every error the same way. I also set the Content-Type header, and keep business logic in a separate service class so it can be reused and unit tested.

q: What APIs does Salesforce provide and when do you use each one?
alt: Name the Salesforce APIs and their use cases
Which API should I use for loading millions of records?
REST API vs Bulk API vs SOAP API vs Streaming API
what is metadata api tooling api graphql api in salesforce
a: The REST API is my default for record CRUD and queries from web and mobile apps. The SOAP API does the same with a WSDL contract for systems that need it. Bulk API 2.0 is for large data loads or extracts, roughly anything beyond a few thousand records, processed asynchronously. Composite resources group several REST calls into one round trip. For events I use the Pub/Sub API, or the older Streaming API, to subscribe to platform events and Change Data Capture. Metadata API deploys and retrieves configuration, Tooling API works with developer artifacts like Apex classes and debug logs, and the GraphQL API lets a client fetch exactly the fields it needs across related objects in one request. For example, a nightly load of 500,000 product prices goes through Bulk API 2.0, while a mobile app updating one visit uses REST.
points: REST/SOAP: record CRUD and queries
Bulk API 2.0: large async loads and extracts
Composite: many operations in one call
Pub/Sub & Streaming: events and CDC
Metadata/Tooling: config & dev tools; GraphQL: precise queries

q: How does Bulk API 2.0 work and how is it different from Bulk API 1.0?

bulk api 1 vs bulk api 2

When do you use Bulk API instead of REST API?
a: Bulk API 2.0 is a REST-based, asynchronous API for loading or extracting large volumes. For ingest, I create a job with the object, operation and external Id field, upload the CSV data, mark the job UploadComplete, then poll until it's complete and download the successful, failed and unprocessed results. The big difference from 1.0 is that 2.0 manages batching for me. I don't create or size batches myself, and query jobs handle chunking automatically. But 2.0 only supports CSV, while 1.0 also supports XML and JSON and lets me choose serial or parallel mode. Say I upsert 300,000 contacts and 1,200 fail. I always process the failedResults file, fix those rows and reload them. I use Bulk API when volumes are big enough that REST would waste API calls.

q: What is the Composite API and how do you create related records in one call?
alt: Explain composite request with referenceId
How can I create an account and contact in a single API call?
composite vs batch vs sobject tree vs collections
How do you reduce the number of API calls from an external system?
a: The Composite resource lets a client send up to 25 subrequests in one call. Later subrequests can reference results from earlier ones with the @{referenceId.field} syntax. Say a website signs up a new customer. In one call I create the Account with referenceId newAcc, then create a Contact with AccountId set to @{newAcc.id}. With allOrNone set to true, if the contact fails, the account rolls back too, so I don't end up with an orphan account. The whole call counts as one API request against limits. Related options: Composite Batch for independent subrequests, sObject Tree for nested record trees, and sObject Collections for up to 200 records of one type in one call. For very large related sets, Composite Graph is the next step.

q: What is the difference between the Streaming API and the Pub/Sub API?
alt: PushTopic vs platform events vs Pub/Sub API
Should I use CometD or Pub/Sub API to subscribe to events?
what is the pub sub api in salesforce
How do external systems listen to Salesforce events?
a: Both let external clients receive events from Salesforce, but the technology is different. The Streaming API is based on CometD long polling over HTTP. It supports PushTopic events, generic events, platform events and Change Data Capture. PushTopic and generic events are legacy and aren't being enhanced. The Pub/Sub API is the newer interface, built on gRPC and HTTP/2 with Avro-encoded payloads. A client can both publish and subscribe through one API. It uses a pull model with flow control, so the client asks for as many events as it can handle, and it's more efficient for high volumes. For example, if a data warehouse needs to consume thousands of change events an hour, with Pub/Sub it can ask for 100 at a time and not get flooded. For new external subscribers, I use the Pub/Sub API.
points: Streaming API: CometD, PushTopic/generic are legacy
Pub/Sub API: gRPC, HTTP/2, Avro
Pub/Sub can publish and subscribe
Client-controlled flow, better for high volume

q: How do subscribers avoid missing events when using platform events or Change Data Capture with the Pub/Sub API?
alt: What is a replay Id and how do you use it?
What happens to events if my subscriber is down?
event retention period for platform events
How do you resume from where you left off after a subscriber crash?
a: Every event has a replay Id, and high-volume platform events and change events are retained for 72 hours. My subscriber stores the replay Id of the last event it processed successfully. If it restarts, it subscribes with that replay Id and gets everything after it, instead of only new events or everything in the window. For example, if the subscriber crashes at 2 a.m. and comes back at 6, it resumes from its saved replay Id and catches up on those four hours. But if it's down longer than the 72-hour window, those events are gone. So I need a fallback, like a reconciliation job or querying changed records. With the Pub/Sub API, managed subscriptions, still in beta, can let Salesforce track the committed replay position for me. And because replays can deliver an event again, processing must be idempotent.
points: Persist last processed replay Id
Retention: 72 hours for high-volume events and CDC
Resubscribe from stored replay Id after downtime
Have a reconciliation fallback; make handlers idempotent

q: What is the Salesforce GraphQL API and when would you use it?

It's built on the UI API, which means it respects field-level security and sharing. In LWC I use the lightning/uiGraphQLApi wire adapter, and external apps call the graphql endpoint under the REST data path. Say a mobile screen needs an account's name, its five latest opportunities, and each opportunity's owner name. With REST that's several calls. With GraphQL it's one query that returns just those fields. I'd use it for UI-driven or mobile scenarios like that, and stay with REST or Bulk for heavy data movement.

q: What are Platform Events and when would you use them?
alt: Explain platform events in Salesforce
What is an event-driven architecture in Salesforce?
platform event use case example
How do you publish and subscribe to platform events?
a: Platform Events are custom event messages, defined like an object with the __e suffix, and used for event-driven integration. A publisher fires an event and doesn't know or care who listens. Subscribers react to it. So systems are loosely coupled. I can publish from Apex, Flow or an external system through the API. I can subscribe with an Apex trigger, a platform event-triggered Flow, LWC using empApi, or externally through the Pub/Sub API. For example, when an order is ready, Salesforce publishes Order_Ready__e. The ERP picks it up and starts fulfilment, and a flow in Salesforce emails the customer. Neither one knows about the other. Other uses are receiving IoT signals or decoupling a heavy process. One thing to remember: events can't be queried or updated like records. They're fire-and-forget messages.
points: Object with __e suffix, publish/subscribe model
Publish: Apex, Flow, APIs
Subscribe: Apex trigger, Flow, LWC empApi, Pub/Sub API
Loose coupling between systems

q: How do you publish a platform event from Apex and subscribe to it with a trigger?
alt: Write code to publish a platform event
EventBus.publish example
platform event trigger example in apex
How do I check if a platform event was published successfully?
a: I create event instances, set their custom fields, and call EventBus.publish with a list. It returns a SaveResult for each event, so I can check for publish errors. On the subscriber side, I write an after insert trigger on the event object. That's the only supported trigger event. The trigger runs asynchronously as the Automated Process user by default, and I can configure a different running user and batch size. Say I publish 500 Payment_Received__e events after a bank file is processed. The subscriber trigger gets them in batches, so it must be bulkified like any trigger, one query and one update for the whole batch. a: An operation is idempotent if doing it twice gives the same result as doing it once. It matters because retries, redelivered events and outbound message retries all cause duplicates. For events, I store processed message or replay Ids and skip ones I've already seen. And I prefer absolute values over incremental ones. For example, 'set status to Shipped' is safe to apply twice. a: The risks show up during bulk updates. A large load runs the trigger in chunks of 200, so one transaction can try to enqueue many jobs and hit the limit of 50 Queueables per transaction. Picture a data fix that updates 100,000 accounts. That would mean hundreds of jobs hammering the ERP at once. To design around it, I'd mark records as pending and let a scheduled or chained job drain them in controlled batches. Or I'd publish platform events or use Change Data Capture and let middleware handle throttling and ordering. I'd add a bypass switch for data migrations, and make the ERP side idempotent.

q: How would you design a nightly sync of one million records from an external system into Salesforce?

a: I'd use the batch data synchronization pattern, with middleware or an ETL tool calling Bulk API 2.0. First, send only deltas using a last-modified watermark instead of the full million every night. Usually only a few thousand records actually change in a day, so that's a big saving. Load with upsert on an External Id, so reruns are safe. Load parents before children, and sort children by parent to reduce record lock contention. For example, load accounts first, then contacts sorted by account, so two batches aren't fighting over the same account. For heavy automation, I'd use a bypass setting for the integration user, or move logic into async processing, so triggers and flows don't slow the load. Afterwards, the middleware reads failed results, retries transient failures and reports the rest. I'd schedule it outside business hours and monitor API and Bulk usage.

q: The external system is sometimes down. How do you retry failed callouts automatically?
alt: Retry callouts using queueable and transaction finalizer
What is a transaction finalizer and how do you use it for retries?
external API is down how do you handle it in apex
exponential backoff retry in salesforce
a: I make the callout in a Queueable and attach a Transaction Finalizer with System.attachFinalizer. If the callout throws, say on a timeout, or a 5xx that I convert into an exception, the finalizer still runs and sees UNHANDLED_EXCEPTION. It then re-enqueues the job with an attempt counter and a delay, using System.enqueueJob with a delay in minutes for backoff. For example, first retry after 1 minute, then 5, then 10. A finalizer can enqueue one job, and a failing Queueable can be re-enqueued by its finalizer up to five times in a row. So after my maximum attempts, I write a failure log and alert someone, instead of retrying forever.

q: How would you design a resilient outbound integration if the target system can be down for hours?
alt: Design for guaranteed delivery when the external system has outages
external system down for a long time, how do you avoid losing data?
dead letter queue in salesforce
retry with platform events and logs
a: Short retries aren't enough for long outages, so I make every outbound change durable. When a record changes, I write it to a sync queue, either a custom staging object or a status field, or I publish a platform event that a subscriber turns into a queue record. A scheduled job picks up pending items, calls out with retries and backoff, and marks them sent, failed-retryable or failed-permanent. After a maximum number of attempts, items go to a dead-letter state with an alert and a reprocess button. Say the ERP is down for six hours overnight. All the changes just pile up in the queue, and when it comes back they go out. Because items are replayed after the outage, I process them in order per record and keep the target idempotent. With middleware, its persistent queues handle much of this.
points: Persist outbound changes in a queue/staging object

Dead-letter state + alert + reprocess
Ordering per record and idempotent target

a: My first choice is declarative. An External Credential using OAuth 2.0 with the JWT bearer flow, or the JWT protocol, with the signing certificate from Certificate and Key Management, and a Named Credential on top. Then the Apex just calls the named credential, and Salesforce mints and refreshes the tokens. If I need custom claims or the setup doesn't fit, I can do it in code. In the test I call Test.setMock with the mock, call the code under test, and assert on the results. For example, for a weather service, one mock returns 200 with a temperature in the JSON, and I assert the record got that temperature. q: Data from two systems keeps overwriting each other in a bidirectional sync. How would you solve it?
alt: bidirectional sync conflict resolution
integration loop where updates bounce back and forth
How do you prevent infinite update loops between Salesforce and an ERP?
two systems updating the same field
a: First I define ownership. Ideally each field has one system of record. So Salesforce owns some fields and the ERP owns others, and each side only sends what it owns. For example, Salesforce owns the account's phone and the ERP owns the credit limit. To stop echo loops, I skip outbound sync when the change was made by the integration user, or compare a last-synced hash or timestamp so unchanged data isn't sent back. Otherwise the ERP updates a record, Salesforce sees a change and sends it back, the ERP sees a change, and it keeps bouncing. Where both sides can edit the same field, I pick a rule like last-writer-wins using a reliable modified timestamp, or send conflicts to a review queue. I also make sure updates are idempotent and ordered per record.
